Hi @LuCazzola, and thank you for the detailed message.
Indeed, traditional models keep the condition (T-pose in our case) unchanged.
However, recently there has been a trend, most notably in models such as FLUX and SD3, where conditional tokens and noisy (generation) tokens attend to each other jointly. As a result, the conditioning (e.g., the T-pose, text) is modified by the generation latent (e.g., motion, image), and vice versa, during attention.
See also: https://blog.sotaaz.com/post/sd3-flux-architecture-en.

title: Inquiry regarding Per-Skeleton vs. Dataset-Level Normalization for Generalization

comments.body:
Dear @sy-hwang,
Thank you for your interest and for sharing custom_bvh.py.
Our BVH code is based on [this implementation](http://theorangeduck.com/page/deep-learning-framework-character-motion-synthesis-and-editing), which is actually quite similar to your custom_bvh.py version. I intentionally modified the original code to represent skeletal end-effectors as BVH End Sites. The reason is that otherwise, a redundant zero-length bone appears in tools like Blender, which I personally prefer to avoid. That said, this is largely a matter of taste, and your approach works perfectly well too.
Note that end-effectors do not contain motion data, since rotation values affect only their predecessors, which end-effectors do not have, so the issue you mentioned does not actually arise.
Regarding skinning, we use the script shared in issue [#25](https://github.com/Anytop2025/Anytop/issues/25), which aligns the skin and changed topology. That said, if you use your custom_bvh.py script, you won’t need the script from issue #25.
In short, there are no action items on your side, just clarifying that both approaches are valid and that the choice mainly comes down to preference.
Best,
Sigal

Addressing related questions:

**Q:** Did you try to run inference on a skeleton from a different dataset, and do you have a sense how well the inference should generalize? 
**A:** We ran inference on skeletons that were held out (i.e., unseen) during the training. Table 2 in our [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.17327) shows that the generalization on unseen skeletons is better when the skeleton is closer to the distribution on which the model has been trained, and gradually drops as they deviate from data distribution.  In this respect, using the quadrupeds model for a wolf (as you did) is the right choice. 

**Q:** We were wondering, for example, if any of the trained models should be applicable to, say, the skeleton of a Wolf model. Do you have tips for normalizations/pre-processing to make the input sufficiently in-distribution?
**A:** For normalization and pre-processing, please follow our [instructions](https://github.com/Anytop2025/Anytop?tab=readme-ov-file#preprocessing-new-skeleton) (from your description, it seems you already did). You might get better results if you include more wolf motions in the preprocessing stage, to get better mean/std values. According to your description, you used only one wolf motion for that. To be clearer, it is better to include as many motions as possible in the preprocessing stage, as long as those motions share the same skeleton and are plaussible.
Foot joints: Foot joints are detected according to their names (i.e., the name that is found in the bvh file). In your specific case, I notice that the back feet are identified, but the front ones are not (marked by green dots). You might want to change the [keywords](https://github.com/Anytop2025/Anytop/blob/dcce5ec71ee84a06233ce4f37614e15f19f5f1d8/data_loaders/truebones/truebones_utils/motion_process.py#L127) to get the front feet identified correctly. 

**Q**: Do you have any tips for training the model on a new dataset of skeleton animations, any difficulties you ran into that we should look out for?
**A:** Here are several tips. 
1. Training the quadrapeds model from scratch, without skeletons that are connected to the ground, may lead to a better model. In order to do so, remove [objects that are connected to the ground](https://github.com/Anytop2025/Anytop/blob/dcce5ec71ee84a06233ce4f37614e15f19f5f1d8/data_loaders/truebones/truebones_utils/param_utils.py#L20C1-L20C20) from the [QUADRUPEDES list](https://github.com/Anytop2025/Anytop/blob/dcce5ec71ee84a06233ce4f37614e15f19f5f1d8/data_loaders/truebones/truebones_utils/param_utils.py#L23C1-L23C11) before training. If you are already training on the quadrupeds dataset, include your wolf in the training as well.
2. If you wish to learn only one motion, it is better to use [SinMDM](https://sinmdm.github.io/SinMDM-page/).
3. If you wish to learn only one skeleton, based on several motions, I can share a private copy of SinMDM that learns from several motions. Contact me at sigal.raab@gmail.com.

title: Question about the model architecture code

comments.body:
In short — our model takes a static skeleton as input and generates a motion sequence for it. However, to remain faithful to the original motion patterns of the given skeleton, it relies on statistical measures (mean and standard deviation) computed from example motions. These statistics are gathered during the new skeleton processing stage, specifically via utils.process_new_skeleton.
If only a single static motion is used to generate this data, the resulting statistics will contain zero rotations, causing the model to produce a static output. To enable the generation of dynamic motions for a previously unseen skeleton, you must provide at least one non-static motion when running utils.process_new_skeleton.

I see, and just to make sure, the output movements are somewhat uncertain, right? The results are more like charater's Idle movements? Is there a way to make the model generate certain kind of movements like resting, running or attacking?

You're correct — we currently don’t support textual control over the generated motion. Introducing more explicit control (e.g., specifying actions like running or attacking) is definitely something we’re considering for future work.

Our BVH I/O implementation requires uniform channel counts across all joints (except the root). This is a technical limitation that hasn't affected users until your case - we apologize for the inconvenience.
As a solution, we suggest you create a preprocessing script to standardize all non-root joints to exactly 3 channels. Don't worry about data loss during this conversion; our system only processes rotational data and automatically disregards positional channel information for joints.

This isn’t an error, but rather the expected logs from the inverse kinematics process. That's a positive indication — the decreasing error suggests that the process is gradually converging.
You can safely disable logging if you prefer a cleaner output.

Could you check how the generated .mp4 or .bvh files look? If they appear correct, then everything likely worked as intended.

Feel free to let us know if you run into any other issues or have questions!

This issue is often caused by a mismatch in the matplotlib version. You have two possible solutions:
-  Downgrade matplotlib to the version in the original environment file:  matplotlib==3.1.3
-  If you prefer not to downgrade matplotlib, modify the [line](https://github.com/Anytop2025/Anytop/blob/b8af0ef6b9f1de7f6ba8d415dd5170c83599b298/data_loaders/truebones/truebones_utils/plot_script.py#L261) from ax = p3.Axes3D(fig) to ax.add_subplot(111, projection='3d')

Let us know if either of these solutions resolves the issue.
Thanks! The videos seem correct containing skeleton movements after downgrading matplotlib.
